catalog_quote: The placement of word stress is not predictable and needs to be remembered for all stems with more than one syllable. For words in isolation it is indicated in the phonemic transcription with an acute above the nucleus vowel of the stressed syllable (´). The acute is omitted on monosyllabic stressed stems in isolation. Stress can be contrastive, but full minimal pairs are rare and usually not valid for more than one dialect. ... Although the position of word stress is not generally predictable, there is a tendency for it to fall on the final stem syllable of a word (before any suffixes, inflectional elements or clitics). ... It is not impossible for lexical stress to fall on a suffix. Stress remains in the same position throughout inflectional paradigms, so that if lexical stress is on the suffix, the suffix will be stressed in all inflectional forms, e.g. mus-é (DIR), mus-ḗ (OBL) 'mous…

new_statements.quote: Three accentual symbols occur before an accented word to denote the position of accent as follows: ` = accent on first syllable, ^ = accent on second syllable, ´ = accent on final syllable (of a word-stem). The latter accent occurs only with polysyllabic words of foreign origin, following the Persian accentual pattern. Alternatively, accent is indicated by an accent mark ( ʹ ) before the accented vowel. [...] Words of foreign origin may be joined in accentual transition by a plus sign , indicating that such words are to be treated as a unit in applying final-syllable accent. [...] The raised tongue root is linked with a raised larynx, producing a characteristic pitch for unstressed vowels of about an octave above the pitch of a relaxed larynx.

One minor point on the locator: Table 1 has no literal cell reading 'Pitch Accent'; 'Pitch' is a rowspan=6…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds Katë with an empty rule and no existing stress statements; Strand supplies the first explicit statement: accent is lexically positioned (first vs. second syllable in native words, final in Persian loans) and is a pitch accent. Nothing to contradict since the catalog rule is blank. Note that the page describes the Kâmviri (Kom) variety of Kati/Kamkata-viri, not Katë as a whole.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Strand lists 'Pitch Accent' among the phonemes of Kâmviri (Table 1). Every accented word carries one accent whose position must be marked lexically: native words have the accent on either the first or the second syllable (two contrasting symbols, ` and ^, are needed), while polysyllabic loanwords from Persian carry final-stem accent after the Persian pattern. The accented syllable is realised by pitch (he uses 'accented/stressed' and 'unstressed' interchangeably), so this is a lexically placed pitch accent rather than a rule-governed stress. No weight condition is mentioned.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. Only expressive lengthening is mentioned: 'in a couple of words the accented vowel may be lengthened with a second stressed peak to indicate exaggeration' (two-topped vowels), which is expressive, not a secondary-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Polysyllabic words of foreign (Persian) origin take final-syllable accent on the word-stem; compound loan phrases joined by '+' are treated as one unit for final-syllable accent. Monosyllables are not discussed separately.
new_statements.identity_note: Strand's page describes Kâmviri (kâmvʹiri), the speech of the Kom of the Bashgal valley (with remarks on Kombřom speakers), one variety of Kati / Kamkata-viri under kati1270; it is not a statement about Katë (Kata-viri) or Mumviri specifically. The Yoshioka note describes Kati of the Bashgal valley as spoken by a Kalasha-area informant in Pakistan.

tone_statements.citation: Halfmann, Jakob. 2024. A Grammatical Description of the Katë Language (Nuristani). PhD dissertation, Universität zu Köln. kups.ub.uni-koeln.de/73732
tone_statements.quote: Like previous researchers, I could not detect any phonemic tone contrasts in Katë.64 Yoshioka (2021) tentatively notes a “high pitch accent”, which would suggest an accent system which primarily makes use of pitch distinctions. According to my impressionistic observations, the marker of prosodic prominence seems to be a typical stress accent, which has the primary phonetic correlates of loudness and higher pitch, possibly also some effect on length. The exact details of how these factors interact remain to be worked out by future research. ... [fn. 64] Iranian and Nuristani languages of the area have not been found to have phonemic tone contrasts.
tone_statements.summary: Author finds no phonemic tone; prominence is a stress accent (loudness, higher pitch), lexically unpredictable and contrastive; he sets aside Yoshioka's tentative 'high pitch accent'.

audit.reasoning: The classification 'lexical' (unpredictable, stored per stem, contrastive, with a stem-final tendency and paradigm-stable position, no tone) rests on a 2024 684-page reference grammar (Cologne PhD, open access at KUPS) which we hold as PDF+text; every sentence of the deciding quotation, the domain quotation and the the secondary-stress rule's retraction claim was found verbatim at the stated sections/pages (2.1.4.1-2.1.4.1.2 pp. 106-108, 2.1.5.1 p. 110). Halfmann is Glottolog's top grammar for the languoid and explicitly reviews all earlier stress remarks (Grjunberg 1980, Fussman 1983, Strand, Yoshioka 2021); No instrumental study
